claims.text: The initially solid Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are phase-pure high-entropy alloys.
The Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles have chemically disordered structures.
Multicomponent mixing produces local chemical heterogeneity in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Local chemical heterogeneity produces uneven interatomic binding strengths.
The nanoparticle surface contains regions with lower interatomic binding energies than the core.
Lower-cohesive-energy surface regions become disordered at lower temperatures than the rest of the nanoparticle.
This early surface disorder forms a liquid-like premelting layer significantly below the bulk melting point.
Differential nanoscale interfacial energies mediate the formation of the premelted surface layer.
The disordered surface layer destabilizes the crystalline core.
Destabilization by the disordered surface layer accelerates the transition to a fully melted state.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles have a lower melting-transition onset than chemically uniform monometallic nanoparticles of similar size.
Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles have a broader melting-transition range than chemically uniform monometallic nanoparticles of similar size.
Premelting will produce a low-temperature endothermic feature detectable by differential scanning calorimetry.
Premelting will produce diffuse surface structural changes detectable by high-resolution TEM and electron diffraction.
Monometallic nanoparticles or simpler compositionally uniform alloys typically have sharper and more uniform melting transitions.
The proposed mechanism primarily applies to nanoparticles approximately 10–50 nm in size.
The proposed mechanism requires heating rates that permit equilibrium or near-equilibrium structural evolution.
Extreme rapid heating or substantially larger particle sizes may produce deviations from the predicted behavior.
